author: cbsaustin
title: Proposed revision of high school social studies standards sparks debate over Islam content
text:
The Texas State Board of Education (SBOE) is scheduled to vote on new social studies standards for high school students this Friday, Sept. 4.
Texas State Board of Education moves closer to a final decision on the high school social studies curriculum. The Texas State Board of Education is scheduled to vote on new social studies standards for high school students this Friday, Sept. 4.
, or TEKS, state standards that outline what Texas public school students should know and be able to do in every grade and in all required subjects.to revise high school social studies TEKS, the standards' outline of content related to Islam has stirred much discussion in Texas' broader political debate about what students learn in the classroom.contain content about early Islam, focusing on military campaigns, slavery, and female captives. The new standards would frame the Sept. 11 attacks as motivated by "radical Islam" rather than focusing on the specific terrorist groups and extremists who were involved.
"The SBOE chose to teach early Islam through military campaigns, slavery, and female captives. That is not history. That is a selective negative caricature of Islam," said Salman Bhojani, who represents District 92 in the Texas House of Representatives.
"Terrorism has no religion. We do not say 'radical Christianity' when a Christian commits an act of violence," Bhojani said.
"No one's trying to marginalize any specific people or groups or anyone like that...there are facts that are just reality," she said. Drogin argues the new standards would provide students with a more comprehensive, chronological understanding of history.
"Once you bring in this classically inspired chronological comprehensive model, we're going to see kids understanding and learning more about history," she said. "Not just names, dates and figures and events, but also the context that truly matters to give them a deep understanding of the ideals that built the West, that built America, and that have made Texas great. ” David DeMatthews, a professor in UT Austin's College of Education, is a former high school social studies teacher.
"You're preparing to understand world events in context," he said. "You are preparing them, also, not to just listen to what they might hear on the news or social media, but to interrogate actual evidence themselves and come up with their own informed opinions rather than relying on the opinions of external folks. "“I think it's narrowing the scope of curriculum," DeMatthews said.
"And it's, at certain instances, really forcing teachers into a box to teach certain historical events and facts, but not teaching them in the broader context. ” Rep. Bhojani said he is not against the teaching of religion as a historical influence, but he wants to see the same standard applied to every faith. He noted that Islamic contributions to science, mathematics and medicine are not included in the revised TEKS.
Meanwhile, Christianity is described as a central influence in the development of Western society, American ideals and the Civil Rights Movement.
"Every religion has a complex history, and the question is whether we teach it fairly or cherry-pick the darkest moments to make one faith look uniquely dangerous," Bhojani said. "That is documented history being erased, and it's not an opinion," he said. "This is not just a Muslim issue, right, because there are African American histories being washed away as well, and so is Latino history.
" If the proposal is approved in Friday's vote, the new standards would be implemented in Texas public high schools beginning in the 2033-34 school year.
